implementation.name: Microsoft Office Visual Basic for Applications
implementation.version_scope: Office VBA getting-started and MsgBox documentation checked on 2026-10-13.

sources.label: Getting started with VBA in Office

fit.text: VBA automates an Office host's object model, such as workbook or document operations; capabilities depend on that application.

prerequisites.text: Use an Office host with VBA and learn its objects, methods and properties; its macro policy governs execution.

execution.text: Procedures run inside the Office application rather than as independent console executables.

behavior.text: Object-model calls act on the host's documents; MsgBox waits for a button and returns the selected button value.

tooling.text: The Visual Basic Editor and macro recorder help inspect procedures and discover host operations.

maintenance.text: Keep the Office application and its object-model reference identified; APIs are not interchangeable across hosts.

costs.text: The cited language documentation establishes no implementation SPDX grant or current Office price; host licensing remains separate.

example.run_instructions: In an Office host whose macro policy permits this code, insert a standard module in the Visual Basic Editor, paste the procedure and run Hello.
example.expected_result: A message dialog displays PLLDN; closing it returns control to the Office host.

fit.text: VBScript can maintain existing Windows Script Host automation; the engine's availability depends on the Windows installation.

prerequisites.text: Understand VBScript syntax and the host's exposed objects; cscript requires an installed script engine.

execution.text: cscript runs .vbs files in a command-line host; wscript is a distinct Windows host.

behavior.text: The host supplies WScript rather than VBScript providing every operating-system function itself.

tooling.text: cscript supports engine selection, arguments and diagnostics; the language reference is archived documentation.

maintenance.text: Microsoft lists VBScript as deprecated and describes a feature-on-demand stage before removal; verify the target Windows image.

costs.text: No implementation SPDX grant or independent engine price is established here; Windows product terms govern the installed component.

example.run_instructions: On Windows with the VBScript engine installed and execution allowed, run cscript //nologo hello.vbs.

implementation.name: GHDL VHDL analyzer and simulator
implementation.version_scope: GHDL 7.0.0-dev documentation checked on 2026-10-13; example uses basic VHDL simulation constructs.

sources.label: GHDL analyze, elaborate and run workflow

fit.text: VHDL models logic circuits and electronic systems; this profile uses GHDL for behavioral simulation.

prerequisites.text: Learn entities, architectures, concurrent signals and testbenches; simulation and physical synthesis are different workflows.

execution.text: GHDL analyzes sources, elaborates a top-level entity and runs the resulting simulation.

behavior.text: Concurrent assignments react to signal changes; testbench assertions can check outputs after simulated time has advanced.

tooling.text: GHDL provides analysis, simulation and synthesis-related tooling; the tutorial separates a design from its input-generating testbench.

maintenance.text: Pin the VHDL standard mode, backend and simulator version; a behavioral check does not establish hardware timing closure.

costs.text: GHDL's compiler grant is GPL-2.0-or-later; runtime libraries and external synthesis tools can have different terms.

example.run_instructions: Run ghdl -a inverter_test.vhdl, then ghdl -e inverter_test, then ghdl -r inverter_test. This is a simulation testbench, not a hardware programming image.
example.expected_result: Checks both Boolean inversion cases and reports two cases passed at simulated time 2 ns.

licenses.scope: The named implementation only; dependencies and host runtimes have separate terms.
licenses.notice: The driver states the version-2-or-later grant; GHDL explicitly warns that some runtime libraries have different terms.

implementation.name: GNOME valac compiler
implementation.version_scope: GNOME Vala compiler and Vala.dev samples checked on 2026-10-13.

sources.label: Vala basic programs and compile workflow

fit.text: Vala targets native applications and libraries, with direct access to C APIs and the GObject type system.

prerequisites.text: Install valac and the C/GLib development environment; learn the binding packages needed by the intended library.

execution.text: valac translates Vala to C and uses native compilation; GTK applications additionally depend on their GTK package.

behavior.text: Classes and interfaces integrate with GObject; procedural functions and type inference are also available.

tooling.text: API binding files describe accessible C libraries; the compiler accepts package selections such as --pkg gtk4.

maintenance.text: Keep compiler, GLib and binding package versions identified; generated C still depends on the linked native libraries.

costs.text: The compiler grant is LGPL-2.1-or-later; GLib, GTK and other libraries require separate component-level review.

example.run_instructions: Compile with valac total.vala, then run the generated total executable using the platform's executable path syntax.

licenses.notice: The valac driver explicitly grants LGPL version 2.1 or later; application code and linked libraries are outside this compiler-source scope.

implementation.name: Icarus Verilog compiler and vvp simulator
implementation.version_scope: Icarus Verilog getting-started documentation checked on 2026-10-13; this example uses basic Verilog constructs.

fit.text: Verilog describes hardware modules; Icarus compiles designs for backends and supports a subset of SystemVerilog.

prerequisites.text: Learn modules, signals and simulated delays; an input-driving testbench is needed to observe circuit behavior.

execution.text: iverilog normally generates vvp format, which the separate vvp runtime executes as a simulation.

behavior.text: Modules form a hierarchy; concurrent signal logic and timed procedural stimulus model different parts of the design.

tooling.text: The compiler accepts multiple source files or command files, and -s selects the simulation's root module.

maintenance.text: Keep the language mode and Icarus version with the design; its README explicitly documents incomplete language coverage.

costs.text: The selected compiler and vvp grants are GPL-2.0-or-later; vendor tools and device libraries have separate terms.

example.run_instructions: Compile with iverilog -o inverter_test.vvp inverter_test.v, then run vvp inverter_test.vvp.
example.expected_result: Displays input=0 output=1 and input=1 output=0 in simulation. This does not establish a synthesized circuit or physical timing.

implementation.name: Visual Basic compiler on .NET
implementation.version_scope: Visual Basic .NET, not classic VB6; selected .NET SDK and supported project templates determine the workflow.

sources.label: Microsoft .NET console tutorial with Visual Basic example

fit.text: Existing .NET code, Windows Forms and libraries. The language strategy does not extend VB into new workloads.

prerequisites.text: Learn .NET objects, modules and event handling; classic BASIC familiarity helps syntax but does not replace these concepts.

execution.text: Create a Visual Basic .NET project and execute it with the selected .NET runtime.

behavior.text: Visual Basic provides object-oriented and event-oriented language features within .NET.

tooling.text: The .NET CLI offers a VB language option for supported templates; Visual Studio is another documented workflow.

maintenance.text: VB syntax remains stable; new runtime features generally receive consumption support without new VB syntax.

costs.text: Covered Roslyn compiler and .NET runtime code use MIT terms; project dependencies and IDE products are separate choices.

example.code:
Module Program
    Sub Main()
        System.Console.WriteLine("PLLDN")
    End Sub
End Module
example.run_instructions: Run dotnet new console -lang VB -o HelloVb. Replace that project's Program.vb with this example, then run dotnet run --project HelloVb.
example.expected_result: Prints PLLDN followed by a newline.

licenses.scope: Roslyn compiler code covered by its MIT grant.
licenses.notice: Compiler terms do not cover every IDE extension or package.

licenses.scope: Runtime code covered by the repository's MIT grant.

implementation.name: WebAssembly Binary Toolkit (WABT)
implementation.version_scope: WABT and core text-format documentation checked on 2026-10-13; example uses baseline i32 instructions.

fit.text: WebAssembly modules are a low-level compilation format; WABT inspects, converts, validates and interprets them.

prerequisites.text: Learn module exports, typed instructions and host imports; install WABT for the text-to-binary workflow.

execution.text: wat2wasm creates a binary module and wasm-interp runs exported functions in its interpreter.

behavior.text: The example uses an i32 operand stack; operating-system services require a host interface rather than implicit availability.

tooling.text: WABT includes wasm-objdump, wasm-validate and conversions between text and binary representations.

maintenance.text: Match enabled WebAssembly features to the intended runtime; experimental proposals are selected through explicit tool options.

costs.text: WABT uses Apache-2.0; browser engines, WASI hosts and compiled application libraries have separate licenses.

example.run_instructions: Run wat2wasm total.wat -o total.wasm, then wasm-interp total.wasm --run-all-exports.
example.expected_result: The exported total function returns the i32 value 5; the interpreter displays that result.

licenses.scope: The named implementation only; dependencies and host runtimes have separate terms.
licenses.notice: This grant covers the selected toolkit; it does not assign a license to the WebAssembly standard or every runtime.

fit.text: XQuery queries and transforms structured data; BaseX adds an XML database, updates, full-text and web-application facilities.

prerequisites.text: Install BaseX and Java 17 or later for the documented distribution; learn sequences and query expressions.

execution.text: The standalone basex command evaluates a query file or string; server and HTTP modes serve different deployment needs.

behavior.text: XQuery expressions return sequences; the 3.1 feature set also includes maps with atomic keys and sequence values.

tooling.text: BaseX provides a desktop GUI, CLI, Java embedding and server interfaces.

implementation.name: Eclipse Xtend compiler
implementation.version_scope: Eclipse Xtend getting-started documentation and Xtext license checked on 2026-10-13.

fit.text: Xtend writes JVM application classes that are translated into Java source, with access to Java projects and libraries.

prerequisites.text: Use an Eclipse Java project with the Xtend SDK and xtend.lib on its classpath; learn classes and method declarations.

execution.text: Eclipse generates Java into xtend-gen; the resulting class runs through the Java application workflow.

behavior.text: A class with a static main method supplies the entry point; utility calls can depend on the Xtend runtime library.

tooling.text: The IDE adds missing runtime libraries through a quick fix and provides introductory example projects.

maintenance.text: Preserve the Xtend compiler and runtime versions alongside the Java toolchain and build configuration.

costs.text: The selected Xtext/Xtend repository uses EPL-2.0; the JDK and project libraries retain separate licenses.

example.run_instructions: Place Hello.xtend in an Eclipse Java project's source folder with the Xtend SDK and xtend.lib configured. Build the project and run the generated Hello class as a Java application.
